Thermal optimization

Source: vignettes/thermal_optimization.Rmd
thermal_optimization.Rmd

Function add_tank_optimization() optimizes a heat pump that charges one thermal tank (e.g. a domestic hot water or a buffer tank), which the heat demand of the building discharges. It solves one independent optimization problem per optimization window (typically one day), with the same objectives, optimization windows and solvers as add_battery_optimization():

  • Minimize the power exchanged with the grid (net power), with opt_objective = "grid" (QP, OSQP)
  • Minimize the energy cost, with opt_objective = "cost" (LP, HiGHS, or QP when lambda > 0)
  • Minimize a weighted combination of net power and cost, with a numeric opt_objective between 0 and 1 (QP)

The tank plays the role of the battery: it stores heat, so the compressor can run when electricity is cheap or locally produced, and the tank delivers the heat later. On top of the compressor, the heat pump can have a resistive backup heater, and the comfort floor of the tank is soft: when neither the compressor nor the backup heater can keep the tank above it, the tank keeps giving heat below its comfort temperature, down to the temperature of the inlet water, and the optimization reports that heat as unmet heat instead of failing. In this article, we’ll cover the tank model, the backup heater and the soft comfort floor, followed by a worked example.

Tank model

The decision variables of every optimization window, with TT time slots of Δt\Delta t hours, are:

  • PtP_t : Electric power of the compressor (kW)
  • BtB_t : Power of the backup heater (kW). It is resistive, so its electric power is also its heat (COP=1COP = 1). Only a variable when the heat pump has a backup heater (Pb > 0)
  • StS_t : Level of the tank at the end of slot tt (kWh thermal): the heat it holds above the inlet temperature, the temperature of the cold water that refills it. At St=0S_t = 0 the tank is at the inlet temperature and gives no more heat

And the parameters:

  • QtQ_t : Heat demand (kW thermal), the column heat_demand of opt_data
  • COPtCOP_t : Coefficient of performance of the compressor, the column cop of opt_data. COPt=0COP_t = 0 means the compressor cannot serve the tank in that slot (e.g. while it defrosts or serves another circuit)
  • TcapT_{cap} : Tank capacity (kWh thermal), Tcap: the heat between the inlet temperature and the top of the tank
  • PcP_c : Maximum electric power of the compressor, Pc
  • PbP_b : Rating of the backup heater, Pb (NULL or 0 without one)
  • SOCminSOC_{min} : Comfort floor of the tank (%), the lowest level that still delivers heat at the comfort temperature
  • SOCmaxSOC_{max} : Top of the tank (%)
  • ll : Standing loss of the tank (% per hour), loss
  • S0S_0 : Level before the first slot of the window

The level of the tank follows the heat balance:

St=St−1(1−l100)Δt+(COPt⋅Pt+Bt−Qt)Δtt∈T S_t = S_{t-1} \left(1 - \frac{l}{100}\right)^{\Delta t} + \left(COP_t \cdot P_t + B_t - Q_t\right) \Delta t \quad t \in T

with the following constraints:

  • The level stays between the comfort floor and the top of the tank. The floor is soft (see Soft comfort floor): the level can go below it, down to the inlet temperature (St=0S_t = 0) at most:

TcapSOCmin100≤St≤TcapSOCmax100t∈T T_{cap} \frac{SOC_{min}}{100} \le S_t \le T_{cap} \frac{SOC_{max}}{100} \quad t \in T

  • The compressor runs between 0 and its maximum power, and not at all where the COP is 0:

0≤Pt≤Pc,Pt=0whereCOPt=0t∈T 0 \le P_t \le P_c, \qquad P_t = 0 \;\; \text{where} \;\; COP_t = 0 \quad t \in T

  • The backup heater runs between 0 and its rating, also where the COP is 0:

0≤Bt≤Pbt∈T 0 \le B_t \le P_b \quad t \in T

  • Every window ends at least as full as it started, so that a window does not empty the tank at the expense of the next one:

ST≥S0 S_T \ge S_0

  • The heat pump’s electric load Pt+BtP_t + B_t is part of the net power of the site, Lt+Pt+Bt−GtL_t + P_t + B_t - G_t, which must stay within the grid import and export capacities, as in the net power article, unless they cannot be met (see Soft grid capacities).

Litres and temperatures

The model counts the heat in the tank in kWh, but a tank is usually described by its volume and its temperatures. Assuming a mixed tank (one temperature for all its water), the heat it holds above the inlet temperature TinT_{in} is:

S=V⋅cp⋅(T−Tin),cp=4.1863600≈0.001163kWh / (L K) S = V \cdot c_p \cdot \left(T - T_{in}\right), \qquad c_p = \frac{4.186}{3600} \approx 0.001163 \; \text{kWh / (L K)}

So a tank of volume VV (L) that can be heated up to TmaxT_{max}, with a comfort floor at TfloorT_{floor}, translates into the arguments of add_tank_optimization() as:

Tcap=V⋅cp⋅(Tmax−Tin),SOCmin=100⋅Tfloor−TinTmax−Tin,SOCmax=100 T_{cap} = V \cdot c_p \cdot \left(T_{max} - T_{in}\right), \qquad SOC_{min} = 100 \cdot \frac{T_{floor} - T_{in}}{T_{max} - T_{in}}, \qquad SOC_{max} = 100

and the level StS_t back into the temperature Tt=Tin+St/(Vcp)T_t = T_{in} + S_t / (V c_p). For example, 300 L between an inlet temperature of 20 °C and a maximum of 55 °C hold 300⋅0.001163⋅35≈12.2300 \cdot 0.001163 \cdot 35 \approx 12.2 kWh, and a comfort floor at 30 °C is SOCmin≈28.6%SOC_{min} \approx 28.6\%.

Optimization windows

The level carries from one window to the next, so the windows are solved in order. They are the windows of the other optimization functions, one every window_days days from window_start_hour, plus the partial windows that the run cuts at both ends:

  • When the first time slot of the run is not a window start (e.g. a run from 00:00 with window_start_hour = 6), the slots up to the first window start form a leading window. It starts from SOCini, and it must also end at least as full as it started.
  • The slots after the last full window form a trailing window.

Both are optimized like any other window. Only the first flex_window_hours of every window are optimized, and the slots after them run the static schedule of the heat pump, the column flexible of opt_data. So with flex_window_hours = 24 (and window_days = 1) every time slot is optimized.

The slots that run flexible behave like the tank too: at the top, the compressor stops as a thermostat would (its power is the static schedule reduced to what keeps the tank at SOCmaxSOC_{max}), and below the comfort floor the tank cools down to the inlet temperature at most, with unmet heat as in the optimized slots.

Objective

The objective is the one of the battery, with the heat pump’s electric load Pt+BtP_t + B_t in place of the battery’s power, plus a linear term on the backup heater. For the net power objective:

minPt,Bt∑t=1T(Lt+Pt+Bt−Gt)2+λ∑t=1T−1(Pt+1−Pt)2+∑t=1T2h⋅Bt \min_{P_t,\, B_t} \; \sum_{t=1}^{T} \left(L_t + P_t + B_t - G_t\right)^2 + \lambda \sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left(P_{t+1} - P_t\right)^{2} + \sum_{t=1}^{T} 2h \cdot B_t

and for the energy cost objective, with the imported power ItI_t and exported power EtE_t of the cost article and It−Et=Lt+Pt+Bt−GtI_t - E_t = L_t + P_t + B_t - G_t:

minPt,Bt,It,Et∑t=1T(It⋅PIt−Et⋅PEt)+λ∑t=1T−1(Pt+1−Pt)2+∑t=1T2h⋅Bt \min_{P_t,\, B_t,\, I_t,\, E_t} \; \sum_{t=1}^{T} \Big( I_t \cdot PI_t - E_t \cdot PE_t \Big) + \lambda \sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left(P_{t+1} - P_t\right)^{2} + \sum_{t=1}^{T} 2h \cdot B_t

The weighted objective combines both as described in the combined optimization article, with the same linear term. When the comfort floor or the grid capacities cannot be held, the window gets the further terms described below.

Compressor first, backup heater second, comfort last

The linear terms order the ways to cover the heat demand. They are built from the heat price hh of the window: the highest value that one kW of electric load can take in the window’s objective, divided by the lowest positive COP when it is below 1, so that no kWh of heat from the compressor is worth more than hh:

Objective Heat price hh
"cost" max⁡t(|PIt|,|PEt|)\max_t \left(\lvert PI_t \rvert, \lvert PE_t \rvert\right), the highest electricity price of the window
"grid" 2(max⁡t|Lt−Gt|+Pc+Pb)2 \left(\max_t \lvert L_t - G_t \rvert + P_c + P_b\right), the largest derivative of the squared net power
weight w w times the grid value (scaled as the net power term) plus 1 - w times the cost value

and with lambda > 0 the largest derivative of the ramping penalty, 4λPc4 \lambda P_c, is added to it. Then:

  • The backup heater pays 2h2h per kW of heat on top of its electricity, which the objective already sees like the compressor’s. Its heat is therefore always more expensive than the compressor’s, so it only runs for the heat the compressor cannot deliver, either because the compressor is at PcP_c, or because its COP is 0. It never runs to absorb a PV surplus or a cheap hour that the compressor could absorb.
  • Missing a grid capacity costs 10h10h per kW (see Soft grid capacities).
  • Going below the comfort floor costs 20h/Δt20h / \Delta t per kWh below it and time slot, more than any kWh of heat the compressor, the backup heater or a missed grid capacity can deliver. So the tank only cools below its floor when they cannot hold it, and is brought back above it as soon as they can.

Soft comfort floor

Without a soft floor, a window where the compressor and the backup heater cannot keep the tank above SOCminSOC_{min} (a cold spell, a compressor too small for the peak, a COP of 0 during a long defrost) would have no solution at all. A real tank, in that case, keeps giving heat: its water gets colder than the comfort temperature, down to the temperature of the inlet water, and from there it gives no more. The optimization does the same. When a window has no solution that holds the floor, it is solved again with:

  • the level between the inlet temperature and the top, 0≤St≤TcapSOCmax1000 \le S_t \le T_{cap} \frac{SOC_{max}}{100};
  • the depth below the floor, Dt≥TcapSOCmin100−StD_t \ge T_{cap} \frac{SOC_{min}}{100} - S_t, priced at 20h/Δt20h / \Delta t per kWh and slot;
  • the end condition ST≥S0S_T \ge S_0 missed by R≥0R \ge 0 at the same price, so that a tank that has been drained does not have to be refilled by the end of the window at any cost.

Every window has a solution then. The unmet heat UtU_t is the heat that would have been required to keep the tank at least at its comfort floor: the extra heat that, added in slot tt, would have stopped the temperature from falling below the comfort temperature (or further below it). It is a missing energy, not a measure of discomfort: it is positive while the temperature is falling below the floor, and 0 again as soon as it stops falling, even if the tank is still below the floor while it warms back up. Its total is the extra heat a larger heat pump or backup heater would have had to deliver. With S̃t=St−1(1−l/100)Δt+(COPtPt+Bt−Qt)Δt\tilde S_t = S_{t-1} (1 - l/100)^{\Delta t} + (COP_t P_t + B_t - Q_t) \Delta t the level the balance asks for (and St=max⁡(S̃t,0)S_t = \max(\tilde S_t, 0) the level the tank reaches):

UtΔt=max⁡(0,min(TcapSOCmin100,St−1(1−l/100)Δt)−S̃t) U_t \, \Delta t = \max\left(0,\; \min\left(T_{cap} \frac{SOC_{min}}{100},\; S_{t-1} (1 - l/100)^{\Delta t}\right) - \tilde S_t\right)

The first term covers the heat the tank gives from below its floor, and the part of S̃t\tilde S_t below 0 the demand it cannot serve at all once it is at the inlet temperature. Standing losses below the floor are not counted.

So in terms of temperature: the backup heater runs when, with the compressor at full power, the temperature of the tank would drop below the comfort floor; and heat is unmet when, even with the backup heater, the temperature drops below the comfort floor, by as much heat as it would have taken to keep it there. The temperature keeps falling with the demand, to the inlet temperature at most. The unmet heat is a report: it is not part of the heat balance of the tank.

The soft floor only enters the problem of a window when the window has no solution that holds the floor. So, without a backup heater and with a band that the compressor can hold, the problem is exactly the one without it.

Soft grid capacities

As for the battery, the grid import and export capacities are soft. When a window has no solution that holds the band within them (e.g. a PV surplus above the export capacity that a full tank cannot absorb, or an import capacity too low to cover the heat demand), it is solved with the soft comfort floor and with a penalised slack on each capacity, stIs^I_t and stEs^E_t:

Lt+Pt+Bt−Gt−stI≤ICt,Gt−Lt−Pt−Bt−stE≤ECt L_t + P_t + B_t - G_t - s^I_t \le IC_t, \qquad G_t - L_t - P_t - B_t - s^E_t \le EC_t

The slack is bounded by how far the site already misses the capacity without the optimization: for import, with the heat pump running its static schedule LFtLF_t; for export, with the heat pump off, since a full tank cannot take any more heat:

0≤stI≤max⁡(0,Lt+LFt−Gt−ICt),0≤stE≤max⁡(0,Gt−Lt−ECt) 0 \le s^I_t \le \max\left(0,\; L_t + LF_t - G_t - IC_t\right), \qquad 0 \le s^E_t \le \max\left(0,\; G_t - L_t - EC_t\right)

It costs 10h10h per kW in the objective, between the backup heater and going below the comfort floor. So the solver uses the compressor and the backup heater to their limits before missing a capacity, and misses an import capacity before letting the tank cool below its floor. The heat pump switched off, with the tank cooling, always fits these bounds, so every window has a solution. When a capacity is still missed, a message says so, and the net power Lt+Pt+Bt−GtL_t + P_t + B_t - G_t shows where.

Results

add_tank_optimization() returns the compressor’s electric power PtP_t (kW), one value per row of opt_data, rounded to 2 decimals. Its attributes hold the rest of the solution, one value per row as well:

Attribute Content
backup_kw Power of the backup heater BtB_t (kW electric, which is also kW thermal). 0 without a backup heater
unmet_heat_kw Unmet heat UtU_t (kW thermal): the heat that would have been required in each slot to keep the tank at least at its comfort floor. Positive while the temperature falls below the floor, 0 while it warms back up

The electric load of the heat pump is the returned power plus attr(P, "backup_kw"). The level of the tank is not returned, but get_tank_level() computes it from the power and the backup heater, stopping at the inlet temperature. get_tank_unmet_heat() computes the unmet heat of any schedule, with the same definition: for example, of the static schedule flexible, to compare it with the optimized one.

A window the solver fails on (a numerical failure, since every window has a solution) runs the static schedule, with a message. With on_failure = "error", it stops with an error naming the window and the solver status instead.

Example

Package flextools provides an example data set of time-series energy and prices profiles, energy_profiles. We will use three days of January 2023 with 15-minute resolution, the building consumption as static load and the solar PV production. The import prices of this data set are sometimes negative, so we cap the export price at the import price (a feed-in tariff that never pays more than importing costs).

The data set has no heat demand, so we build one with a morning and an evening peak, around a base of 2 kW. The second day is a cold morning: its morning peak reaches 12 kW, far above what the compressor can deliver. The COP of the compressor is 3.2, and drops to 2.7 on the cold day:

opt_data <- energy_profiles %>%
  filter(
    datetime >= dmy("09/01/2023", tz = "CET"),
    datetime < dmy("12/01/2023", tz = "CET")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    day = as.integer(date(datetime) - dmy("09/01/2023")) + 1,
    hour = hour(datetime) + minute(datetime) / 60
  ) %>%
  transmute(
    datetime,
    production = solar,
    static = building,
    price_imported,
    price_exported = pmin(price_exported, price_imported),
    heat_demand = 2 +
      ifelse(
        day == 2,
        10 * exp(-((hour - 8) / 2)^2), # cold morning
        2.5 * exp(-((hour - 7.5) / 1.2)^2)
      ) +
      3 * exp(-((hour - 19) / 1.5)^2),
    cop = ifelse(day == 2, 2.7, 3.2),
    flexible = heat_demand / cop
  )

head(opt_data)
## # A tibble: 6 × 8
##   datetime            production static price_imported price_exported
##   <dttm>                   <dbl>  <dbl>          <dbl>          <dbl>
## 1 2023-01-09 00:00:00          0   1.65         0.0644          0.025
## 2 2023-01-09 00:15:00          0   1.64         0.0644          0.025
## 3 2023-01-09 00:30:00          0   1.63         0.0644          0.025
## 4 2023-01-09 00:45:00          0   1.62         0.0644          0.025
## 5 2023-01-09 01:00:00          0   1.61         0.0603          0.025
## 6 2023-01-09 01:15:00          0   1.57         0.0603          0.025
## # ℹ 3 more variables: heat_demand <dbl>, cop <dbl>, flexible <dbl>

The static schedule flexible is the heat pump following the heat demand without any storage:

The heat pump has a 2 kW compressor and a 300 L tank that can be heated up to 55 °C, with a comfort floor at 30 °C, refilled with inlet water at 20 °C. We convert them into the tank’s capacity and comfort floor as described above:

volume <- 300 # L
T_in <- 20 # °C, inlet water
T_floor <- 30 # °C, comfort floor
T_max <- 55 # °C
kwh_per_degree <- volume * 4.186 / 3600 # kWh per °C

Tcap <- kwh_per_degree * (T_max - T_in)
SOCmin <- 100 * (T_floor - T_in) / (T_max - T_in)
c(Tcap = Tcap, SOCmin = SOCmin)
##     Tcap   SOCmin 
## 12.20917 28.57143

The tank always holds its 300 L, since the inlet water refills whatever is drawn: it is its temperature that tells how much heat it holds. From 55 °C down to the 30 °C floor it can give 8.7 kWh at a comfortable temperature, and 3.5 kWh more, colder, down to the 20 °C of the inlet water. On the cold morning the compressor delivers at most 2.7⋅2=5.42.7 \cdot 2 = 5.4 kW of heat: not enough for the peak.

To show the results, a small helper gathers the compressor power, the backup heater, the unmet heat and the temperature of the tank (from the level that get_tank_level() computes) for each scenario:

tank_results <- function(opt_data, P) {
  opt_data %>%
    mutate(
      P = P,
      B = attr(P, "backup_kw"),
      U = attr(P, "unmet_heat_kw"),
      level = get_tank_level(
        P, heat_demand, cop,
        init = Tcap, time_resolution = 15,
        backup = B
      ),
      temperature = T_in + level / kwh_per_degree
    )
}

daily_totals <- function(results) {
  results %>%
    group_by(date = date(datetime)) %>%
    summarise(
      demand_kWh = sum(heat_demand) / 4,
      compressor_kWh = sum(P) / 4,
      backup_kWh = sum(B) / 4,
      unmet_kWh = sum(U) / 4,
      min_temp_C = min(temperature)
    )
}

Without backup heater

First, the heat pump has no backup heater and minimizes the energy cost:

P <- add_tank_optimization(
  opt_data,
  opt_objective = "cost",
  Tcap = Tcap,
  Pc = 2,
  SOCmin = SOCmin
)
## ⚠️ Optimization warning: the tank goes below its comfort floor in some slots. That heat is unmet (attribute `unmet_heat_kw`).
results <- tank_results(opt_data, P)
daily_totals(results)
## # A tibble: 3 × 6
##   date       demand_kWh compressor_kWh backup_kWh unmet_kWh min_temp_C
##   <date>          <dbl>          <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>
## 1 2023-01-09       61.3           19.2          0      0          30.0
## 2 2023-01-10       91.4           32.3          0      7.59       20  
## 3 2023-01-11       61.3           19.2          0      0          30.0

On the first and the last day, the compressor heats the tank up to 55 °C during the cheapest hours before each peak, and the tank covers the peaks without dropping below 30 °C. On the cold morning the tank starts full, and the compressor runs at full power through the peak, but the temperature falls below the comfort floor at around 08:00 and down to the inlet temperature (20 °C) at around 09:00, where the tank gives no more heat. The unmet heat is the heat that would have been needed to keep the tank at 30 °C: the heat the tank gives below 30 °C, and the demand it cannot serve at all at 20 °C. It follows how fast the temperature falls below the floor, not how far below it is: it ends when the temperature stops falling, at the end of the peak, while the compressor is still bringing the tank back above its floor.

With a backup heater

Now the heat pump also has a 1.5 kW backup heater (Pb = 1.5):

P_backup <- add_tank_optimization(
  opt_data,
  opt_objective = "cost",
  Tcap = Tcap,
  Pc = 2,
  SOCmin = SOCmin,
  Pb = 1.5
)
## ⚠️ Optimization warning: the tank goes below its comfort floor in some slots. That heat is unmet (attribute `unmet_heat_kw`).
results_backup <- tank_results(opt_data, P_backup)
daily_totals(results_backup)
## # A tibble: 3 × 6
##   date       demand_kWh compressor_kWh backup_kWh unmet_kWh min_temp_C
##   <date>          <dbl>          <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>
## 1 2023-01-09       61.3           19.2       0         0          30.0
## 2 2023-01-10       91.4           31.4       6.76      1.95       24.4
## 3 2023-01-11       61.3           19.2       0         0          30.0

The compressor runs as before, and the backup heater switches on when the compressor at full power can no longer keep the tank above the comfort floor during the cold morning. The optimization looks ahead: it starts the backup heater as soon as the peak starts, rather than when the tank reaches 30 °C, because the heat it adds early is kept in the tank for later. The tank now reaches its comfort floor later, at around 08:45, and only then is heat unmet: the tank cools to about 24 °C, and the unmet heat is the heat that, on top of the compressor and the backup heater, would have kept it at 30 °C. It stops when the temperature reaches its lowest point. Right after the peak, the backup heater keeps running with the compressor until the tank is back above its floor. On the first and the last day the compressor suffices, and the backup heater stays off even though it could run in cheaper hours.

With a larger backup heater (e.g. Pb = 3), the tank stays above its floor and the unmet heat disappears altogether.
